subject: chemistry
title: Predicting feasibility from electrode potentials
key_idea: A reaction is thermodynamically feasible when Eᶿcell is positive. Eᶿ values also rank oxidising and reducing agents. A feasible reaction may still not happen, because it can be too slow or the conditions are not standard.

sections.heading: Using Eᶿ values to predict reactions

blocks.text: Eᶿ values show which species gain electrons more easily. This section covers how to use them to predict direction, polarity and feasibility.

items: The half-cell with the **more positive** Eᶿ is reduced. It is the positive electrode.
The half-cell with the **more negative** Eᶿ is oxidised. It is the negative electrode.
Eᶿcell = Eᶿ(reduced) − Eᶿ(oxidised). If Eᶿcell is positive, the reaction is feasible.
In a simple cell, electrons flow in the external wire from the negative electrode to the positive electrode.

items.text: Write both with their Eᶿ values, as reductions.
The more positive Eᶿ is reduced. Reverse the other half-equation.
Cancel the electrons to give the overall equation.
Eᶿ(more positive) − Eᶿ(more negative). A positive value means feasible.

diagram.alt: Pick a reaction and see whether it is feasible from the electrode potentials.

options.label: Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq)
options.explanation: Eᶿcell is positive, so zinc displaces copper.

options.label: Cu(s) + Zn²⁺(aq)
options.explanation: Eᶿcell is negative, so copper does not displace zinc.

options.label: 2Fe³⁺(aq) + 2I⁻(aq)
options.explanation: Fe³⁺ oxidises I⁻ to I₂, so Eᶿcell is positive.

options.label: 2Fe²⁺(aq) + Br₂(aq)
options.explanation: Bromine is a stronger oxidising agent than Fe³⁺.

options.label: Fe²⁺(aq) + Ag⁺(aq)
options.explanation: A very small positive Eᶿcell. The reaction does not go far.

items: The more positive the Eᶿ, the stronger the oxidising agent on the left of the half-equation.
The more negative the Eᶿ, the stronger the reducing agent on the right of the half-equation.
Example: MnO₄⁻/Mn²⁺ is +1.51 V, so MnO₄⁻ is a stronger oxidising agent than Cl₂ (+1.36 V).
A positive Eᶿcell means the reaction is feasible.
The more positive Eᶿ is, the stronger the oxidising agent.
Electrons flow from the negative to the positive electrode.

blocks.text: Eᶿ values show when a species can react with itself. A species disproportionates if it is both a strong enough oxidising agent and reducing agent.

items: Cu⁺ + e⁻ ⇌ Cu, Eᶿ = +0.52 V.
Cu²⁺ + e⁻ ⇌ Cu⁺, Eᶿ = +0.15 V.
Cu⁺ is reduced in the first half-equation and oxidised in the second.
Eᶿcell = +0.52 − (+0.15) = +0.37 V. This is positive, so 2Cu⁺ → Cu + Cu²⁺ is feasible.
If the Eᶿ for the species reduced is more positive than for the species oxidised, it disproportionates.
Copper(I) disproportionates in aqueous solution.

blocks.text: Eᶿ values only tell you about thermodynamics under standard conditions. This section covers the limits.

items: **Kinetic inhibition**: a reaction with a positive Eᶿcell can have a very high activation energy, so it is too slow to see. Example: manganate(VII) and water.
**Non-standard conditions**: the real concentration, temperature or pressure can differ from standard values, which shifts E and may change the sign of Ecell.
Eᶿcell says nothing about the rate of a reaction.

blocks.text: Eᶿcell, entropy and the equilibrium constant
A positive Eᶿcell is the same as a positive total entropy change. It is also linked to the size of the equilibrium constant.

items: Eᶿcell is directly proportional to the total entropy change and to ln K.
A large positive Eᶿcell means a large K, so the reaction goes almost to completion.
A feasible reaction can still be slow, because of kinetic inhibition.
Conditions that are not standard change E.
Eᶿcell is proportional to ln K and to the total entropy change.

checks.q: Use Eᶿ(Ag⁺/Ag) = +0.80 V and Eᶿ(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V to decide whether copper reacts with silver nitrate solution.
checks.a: Eᶿcell = +0.80 − (+0.34) = +0.46 V. This is positive, so copper displaces silver and the reaction is feasible.

checks.q: Give two reasons why a reaction with a positive Eᶿcell may not occur as predicted.
checks.a: The reaction may be too slow because of a high activation energy (kinetic inhibition). The conditions may not be standard, for example a different concentration or temperature.

checks.q: Eᶿ(Cl₂/Cl⁻) = +1.36 V and Eᶿ(Br₂/Br⁻) = +1.07 V. Which is the stronger oxidising agent and which halide ion is the stronger reducing agent?
checks.a: Cl₂ is the stronger oxidising agent (more positive Eᶿ). Br⁻ is the stronger reducing agent than Cl⁻.

blocks.text: The position of the equilibrium Mⁿ⁺ + ne⁻ ⇌ M shifts when the ion concentration changes.

items: A higher concentration of the oxidised ion shifts the equilibrium to the right. E becomes more positive.
A lower concentration of the oxidised ion shifts it to the left. E becomes more negative.

blocks.label: Nernst equation at 298 K
blocks.formula: E = Eᶿ + (0.059 / z) × log([oxidised species] / [reduced species])
where: E is the electrode potential in V and Eᶿ is the standard value in V.
z is the number of electrons in the half-equation.
A pure solid, such as Cu(s), is left out.

items: If [Cu²⁺] = 0.010 mol/dm³, then log = −2 and E = 0.34 − 0.059 = +0.28 V.

blocks.label: Free energy change
where: ΔGᶿ is the standard free energy change in J/mol.
n is the number of moles of electrons transferred in the equation.
Eᶿcell is in V and F is the Faraday constant, 96 500 C/mol.

blocks.text: A positive Eᶿcell gives a negative ΔGᶿ, so the reaction is feasible. Example: Zn + Cu²⁺, n = 2, Eᶿcell = +1.10 V, ΔGᶿ = −2 × 1.10 × 96 500 = −212 kJ/mol.
